The peak ground reaction is 3.3× body weight; the leg spring recoils at 1.46 m/s while the fibre shortens at only 0.44 m/s, a $3.3\times$ speed amplification (Fig. 22, blue tracks the dashed whole-unit while red stays flat near zero); and over the bounce the spring banks $197\ \text{J}$ while the muscle does $6.8\ \text{J}$ of work, so $97\%$ of the push-off is elastic recoil and the muscle mostly holds force. Be exact about near-isometric, because the simulation is: the fibre is not still. It shortens $18\ \text{mm}$ over the stance, a third of its optimal length $\ell_0$, and its length factor $f_L$ falls from $1.00$ to $0.57$ on the way. What is near zero is its velocity at push-off: at the recoil peak it shortens at $0.07\ \text{m/s}$, $0.05$ of the spring's $1.46\ \text{m/s}$ (the block's printed $0.30$ compares the two peaks, which occur at different times). That is the catapult of §4 emerging from the coupled dynamics, and it settles Module 5's Assumption 7.1 debt (b), the fibre–tendon speed difference, with a computed result rather than an argument.

Lab 3 — A ligament constraint under joint motion

Finally the one-sided constraint of §8. Send a limb rotating fast toward over-flexion and let the ligament stop it: the restoring torque is zero until the joint passes the ligament's engagement angle, then rises steeply (Eq. 8.1), decelerating and rebounding the limb — a joint hitting its ligamentous end-stop. Integrating $I\ddot\theta=-T_{\text{lig}}(\theta)$ for three ligament laxities turns the model into a sensitivity study.

import numpy as np
# a limb rotating fast toward over-flexion; a one-sided ligament stops
# it past the limit. Assumed values. Lemma 1 with a power-law toe
# gives T = R k (theta - theta_hi)^p, so k is in N/rad^p.
# segment inertia (kg m^2), moment arm (m), toe constant, exponent
I, R, k, p = 0.20, 0.03, 4.5e6, 2


def run(slack_deg):
    th_hi = np.radians(140 + slack_deg)  # laxity shifts the engagement angle
    dt = 1e-4
    th, w = np.radians(110), np.radians(650)
    peak = np.degrees(th)
    for _ in range(3000):
        over = th - th_hi
        T = R*k*over**p if over > 0 else 0.0  # one-sided (past limit)
        w += (-T/I)*dt
        th += w*dt
        peak = max(peak, np.degrees(th))
    return peak - 140  # overshoot past the ligament limit


for slack in (0, 8, 16):
    print(f"slack +{slack:2d} deg -> overshoot {run(slack):.1f} deg")

A normal ligament arrests the joint after only $\approx3.8^\circ$ of overshoot; loosening it by $16^\circ$ lets the joint fly $\approx19.8^\circ$ past the limit before the steep one-sided torque catches it. The sweep quantifies why laxity — from a previous sprain, or from constitutional hypermobility — raises the risk of over-flexion injury: a slack ligament engages later, and with no torque in the free range the joint still reaches it at the same $650^\circ/\text{s}$, so the same $\approx3.8^\circ$ arrest leaves it further past the normal limit and deeper in the danger zone.

Three integrations, three closed debts: the tendon returns its energy minus a small viscoelastic loss (Lab 1), the muscle–tendon unit banks and returns running energy as a catapult with the fibre's peak speed a third of the spring's peak recoil speed (Lab 2, settling Module 5), and the one-sided ligament constrains a joint's range (Lab 3, §8). §10 now audits what the whole picture still leaves out, and sets the problems.

10. What the model captures and misses; diagnostics and problems

The passive-tissue model earns its place the same way Module 5's did: a handful of measured constants — a collagen modulus, a cross-section, a toe strain, two viscoelastic time constants — turn an elongation into a force, an energy, and a joint constraint, with no free curve-fitting. Be equally clear about what it leaves out. Each idealisation is honest, and each is repaid in a later module (Fig. 24).

What it captures. The J-shaped stress–strain law from crimp and fibre recruitment (§1), the tendon as a structural nonlinear spring with a tangent stiffness that rises through the toe (§2), the elastic energy it stores and returns (§3), the series coupling to Module 5's muscle and the catapult it enables (§4), the creep, relaxation and rate-dependence of real tissue (§5) through the Maxwell / Kelvin–Voigt / standard-linear-solid constitutive laws (§6), the hysteresis loop and its dissipated energy (§7), and the one-sided ligament constraint, the ligament-steered joint axis, and the arch as a tension truss (§8). That is enough to predict, for a given elongation history, the force a tendon carries, the energy it banks, and the range a ligament allows.

What it idealises, and where it is repaid:

Idealisation (in this module)What it omitsRepaid in
The tissue as a one-dimensional lumped spring (§2)whole-body dynamics: the leg as a spring–mass hopper, stance and flight, gait energeticsModule 9 (running / jumping SLIP)
Fixed material constants; small strain (§1, §6)damage accumulation, creep-to-rupture, fatigue, ageing and training adaptation of collagenModule 14
Linear viscoelasticity about an operating point (§6)finite-strain nonlinearity, the full relaxation spectrum, and the fluid–solid (poroelastic) coupling of hydrated collagenModule 16 (continuum)
Planar crossed-cruciate four-bar (§8)the three-dimensional envelope of knee laxity, coupled rotations, and cartilage contactModule 16, later joint chapters

How the tissue is measured and validated

Every quantity in the model maps to a laboratory measurement, which is what keeps it falsifiable:

  • Stress–strain and stiffness — a materials testing machine pulls an excised tendon (or a bone–tendon–bone preparation) and records force against grip-to-grip elongation, tracing the toe and linear regions of §1–§2.
  • In-vivo strain — B-mode ultrasound tracks the Achilles free-tendon length during hopping and running, giving the working strain (a few percent) and the elastic energy of §3.
  • Time constants and hysteresis — a dynamic mechanical analyser imposes sinusoidal strain over a frequency sweep and reads the storage and loss moduli $E',E''$ and $\tan\delta$ (§7), from which $\tau_\sigma,\tau_\varepsilon$ follow.
  • Joint constraint and laxity — an arthrometer (or instrumented laxity test) loads a joint at end-range and measures the displacement, calibrating the one-sided torque of §8.

Diagnostics

Five quick self-checks. Answer each before opening the solution; if any is unclear, the linked section is where to look.

  1. A rubber band gets no harder to stretch as you pull; a tendon does. Why?
    Solution
    A tendon starts with wavy crimp: at first only a few straightened fibrils bear load, so it is compliant (the toe), and as strain grows more fibrils recruit and the tangent stiffness rises toward $k_{\text{lin}}$ (§1, §2). The rising slope of the J-curve is the increasing resistance you feel.
  2. Two runners stretch the Achilles to the same peak force, storing the same energy. One returns more of it on push-off. What differs?
    Solution
    Their resilience — the fraction returned rather than dissipated as heat (§3, §7). A tendon with a smaller hysteresis loop (lower loss tangent) hands back more of the stored energy; the difference is architecture and hydration, not the peak load.
  3. A wallaby hops faster and faster with almost no rise in metabolic cost. How?
    Solution
    Most of the step's energy is banked in the tendon on landing and returned on take-off (§3), while the muscle stays nearly isometric and cheap (§4). The spring, not the motor, supplies the bounce, so raising speed costs little extra chemical energy.
  4. You hold a stretched tendon at a fixed length and the force slowly sags. Which lumped model reproduces this, and which cannot?
    Solution
    This is stress relaxation. The standard linear solid and the Maxwell element both relax (Maxwell all the way to zero, the SLS to a finite plateau); the Kelvin–Voigt solid cannot — at fixed strain its dashpot is idle and the stress stays put (§6).
  5. A previously sprained ankle "gives way" more easily. In terms of the one-sided constraint, what changed?
    Solution
    The ligament became lax: its slack range widened, so the free interval $[\theta_{\text{lo}},\theta_{\text{hi}}]$ of the one-sided torque (§8, Eq. 8.1) is larger. The restoring torque engages later and further into range, so the joint reaches its collision faster and travels deeper before being caught.

Problems

Thirty problems in three strands — conceptual (C1–C10), derivational (D1–D10), and computational (K1–K10) — each with a worked solution; every computational solution ships the Python that prints its numbers. A Probes note names what each tests. The map below shows which section each problem draws on, and, read by row, that every section is exercised — §5 through the models it feeds in §6:

Conceptual (C1–C10)

C1. Why is a tendon's stress–strain curve J-shaped (concave-up) rather than the straight Hookean line of an ideal spring? Probes: crimp and recruitment, §1.
Solution
At rest the collagen fibrils are wavy (crimp). Under load they straighten and begin to bear tension a few at a time (recruitment), so at small strain only a fraction of the tissue resists — the compliant toe — and the tangent stiffness climbs as more fibrils engage, reaching the constant linear slope once all are straight. A concave-up curve is the signature of progressive recruitment (§1).
C2. Tendon, ligament, and fascia are built from the same collagen, yet tendon is the stiffest and most efficient spring of the three along its load axis. What structural feature sets it apart? Probes: tissue architecture, §1.
Solution
Alignment. A tendon's fibrils run nearly parallel to its long axis, so almost every fibre pulls along the load; a ligament is less strictly aligned (it must resist several directions), and fascia is a planar sheet with fibres in-plane at a spread of angles. The same molecules, packed in line, give a stiffer, lower-loss, more nearly one-dimensional spring (§1).
C3. For a nonlinear spring the "stiffness" is not a single number. Define the two stiffnesses that matter, and say which one governs small vibrations about a loaded state. Probes: tangent vs secant stiffness, §2.
Solution
The secant stiffness $F/x$ (the chord slope) sets the average force at a given stretch; the tangent stiffness $k(x)=\mathrm{d}F/\mathrm{d}x$ (the local slope, Eq. 2.2) sets the resistance to a small extra displacement. Small oscillations about a working point see the tangent stiffness, so a tendon held in its stiff linear region vibrates faster than one slack in the toe (§2).
C4. A tendon returns about $93\%$ of the energy it stores; a ligament returns much less, though both are collagen. Why? Probes: resilience and hysteresis, §3, §7.
Solution
Return fraction is resilience $=1-$ (loop area)$/$(stored energy) (§3, §7). A tendon's aligned, well-hydrated, low-loss structure traces a thin hysteresis loop (small $\tan\delta$), so little is lost to heat; a ligament, less strictly ordered, dissipates a larger fraction each cycle. Same collagen, different loss angle — the tendon is tuned to give energy back, the ligament to absorb and stabilise.
C5. A muscle fibre's peak shortening speed is only a few fibre-lengths per second, yet the ankle extends explosively in a jump. How does the series tendon let the joint out-run the fibre? Probes: the catapult, §4.
Solution
The fibre first stretches the tendon slowly, doing work against it while nearly isometric (cheap, high-force). Released, the tendon recoils on its own fast timescale, adding its stored velocity to the fibre's: by Eq. 4.4, $\dot L_{\text{MTU}}=\dot\ell\cos\theta_p+\dot x$, and the tendon term $\dot x$ can dominate. The joint moves at the sum, so it out-runs the fibre — the catapult (§4).
C6. In what limit does the series-elastic MTU reduce to Module 5's rigid-tendon model, and what capability is lost there? Probes: the stiff limit, §4 (Prop. 4).
Solution
As tendon stiffness $k_T\to\infty$ the tendon stretch $x=F/k_T\to0$, so $L_{\text{MTU}}=\ell\cos\theta_p+L_{Ts}$ exactly — the fibre length is slaved to the (measurable) MTU length and Module 5's explicit ODE returns (Prop. 4). What is lost is elastic energy storage and the fibre–tendon speed difference: with no compliance there is no spring to bank energy and no catapult (§4).
C7. Creep and stress relaxation are two experiments on the same tissue. State what is held fixed and what is measured in each, and why one material shows both. Probes: the two step tests, §5.
Solution
Creep: hold the stress constant, watch the strain grow. Relaxation: hold the strain constant, watch the stress decay. Both arise because the tissue has a spring in it (an instantaneous elastic response) and a dashpot (a slow viscous rearrangement): the spring sets the immediate response, the dashpot lets it drift toward equilibrium over the material's time constants (§5).
C8. Kelvin–Voigt cannot reproduce stress relaxation, and Maxwell cannot reproduce a bounded creep. Explain each failure, and how the standard linear solid fixes both. Probes: model structure, §6.
Solution
Kelvin–Voigt (spring ∥ dashpot): at fixed strain the dashpot carries no rate, so the stress equals the spring's and never decays — no relaxation. Maxwell (spring – dashpot in series): under fixed stress the dashpot flows forever, so strain grows without bound — no equilibrium, unbounded creep. The SLS adds a second spring so there is both an instantaneous stiffness and a finite equilibrium: it relaxes to a plateau and creeps to a bound (§6, Eq. 6.3).
C9. Low hysteresis makes a good energy-return spring; high hysteresis makes a good shock absorber. Name a tissue best served by each, and say why the same collagen family spans both. Probes: the loss–return trade-off, §7.
Solution
A tendon (Achilles) wants low loss, to give the stride's energy back; an intervertebral disc or the heel pad (and, in part, a ligament) wants high loss, to soak up impact and protect the joint. The loss tangent is set by how much viscous rearrangement the architecture and hydration allow: aligned, cross-linked tendon dissipates little; looser, more hydrated tissue dissipates much — one material family, tuned across the spectrum (§7).
C10. The knee is often drawn as a hinge with a fixed axis. Why does its true flexion axis migrate, and what ligament structure sets the path? Probes: the crossed four-bar, §8.
Solution
The two cruciate ligaments cross, forming a four-bar linkage (femoral link, tibial link, and the two crossed cruciates). Its instant centre — the momentary axis of rotation — sits at the cruciate crossing (Prop. 10) and moves as the bars swing, so the axis migrates and the contact rolls then glides. Ligament geometry, not a fixed pin, sets the path (§8).

Derivational (D1–D10)

D1. Take recruitment to be linear: the engaged fibril fraction is $\Phi(\varepsilon)=\varepsilon/\varepsilon^\ast$ up to $\varepsilon^\ast$, then $1$. Derive the toe stress $\sigma(\varepsilon)=E_{\text{lin}}\varepsilon^2/(2\varepsilon^\ast)$ and show $\sigma$ and its slope are continuous at $\varepsilon^\ast$. Probes: §1 (Prop. 1).
Solution
With $E(\varepsilon)=E_{\text{lin}}\Phi$, $\sigma=\int_0^\varepsilon E_{\text{lin}}(\varepsilon'/\varepsilon^\ast)\,\mathrm{d}\varepsilon'=E_{\text{lin}}\varepsilon^2/(2\varepsilon^\ast)$ for $\varepsilon\le\varepsilon^\ast$. At $\varepsilon^\ast$ this gives $\sigma=E_{\text{lin}}\varepsilon^\ast/2$ and slope $\mathrm{d}\sigma/\mathrm{d}\varepsilon=E_{\text{lin}}$; the linear branch $\sigma=E_{\text{lin}}\varepsilon^\ast/2+E_{\text{lin}}(\varepsilon-\varepsilon^\ast)$ matches both value and slope there, so the J-curve is $C^1$ (Eq. 1.2).
D2. From the material law $\sigma(\varepsilon)$ derive the structural force $F(x)=A_0\,\sigma(x/L_0)$ and the tangent stiffness $k(x)$; show $k$ rises from $0$ through the toe to the constant $k_{\text{lin}}=A_0E_{\text{lin}}/L_0$. Probes: §2 (Prop. 2).
Solution
Force is stress times rest area, $F=A_0\sigma(\varepsilon)$ with $\varepsilon=x/L_0$ (Eq. 2.1). Then $k=\mathrm{d}F/\mathrm{d}x=A_0(\mathrm{d}\sigma/\mathrm{d}\varepsilon)(1/L_0)=(A_0/L_0)E(\varepsilon)$ (Eq. 2.2). In the toe $E=E_{\text{lin}}\varepsilon/\varepsilon^\ast$ rises linearly from $0$; past $\varepsilon^\ast$, $E=E_{\text{lin}}$ so $k=k_{\text{lin}}=A_0E_{\text{lin}}/L_0$, constant.
D3. Derive the linear elastic energy $U=\tfrac12kx^2=F^2/(2k)$ three ways — by integrating $F\,\mathrm{d}x$, as the area of a triangle, and from the force. Then give the toe energy $U(x^\ast)=\tfrac16k_{\text{lin}}(x^\ast)^2$. Probes: §3 (Prop. 3).
Solution
(i) $U=\int_0^x kx'\,\mathrm{d}x'=\tfrac12kx^2$. (ii) The $F$–$x$ line has height $F=kx$ over base $x$; triangle area $=\tfrac12Fx=\tfrac12kx^2$. (iii) $x=F/k$ gives $U=\tfrac12k(F/k)^2=F^2/(2k)$ (Eq. 3.2). For the toe, $F=k_{\text{lin}}x^2/(2x^\ast)$, so $U(x^\ast)=\int_0^{x^\ast}k_{\text{lin}}x'^2/(2x^\ast)\,\mathrm{d}x'=\tfrac16k_{\text{lin}}(x^\ast)^2$ (Eq. 3.3): the concave toe stores only a third of the $\tfrac12k_{\text{lin}}(x^\ast)^2$ a linear spring would.
D4. Show the resilience $R=U_{\text{returned}}/U_{\text{stored}}$ equals $1-$ (loop area)$/U_{\text{stored}}$, and relate it to the loss angle $\delta$ for small loss. Probes: §3, §7.
Solution
Over a load–unload cycle the energy in is the area under the loading curve $U_{\text{stored}}$; the energy out is the area under the unloading curve $U_{\text{ret}}=U_{\text{stored}}-W_d$, where $W_d=\oint\sigma\,\mathrm{d}\varepsilon$ is the enclosed loop area (Eq. 7.1). Hence $R=1-W_d/U_{\text{stored}}$. For the tendon's tension cycle $0\to\varepsilon_0\to0$ (amplitude $\varepsilon_0/2$, as in the figure and K8), $W_d=\pi E''(\varepsilon_0/2)^2$ and $U_{\text{stored}}\approx\tfrac12E'\varepsilon_0^2$, so $R\approx1-\tfrac{\pi}{2}(E''/E')=1-\tfrac{\pi}{2}\tan\delta$ for small $\tan\delta$ — low loss angle, high return.
D5. Two springs (fibre $k_M$, tendon $k_T$) in series carry one force. Derive the series stiffness $1/k=1/k_M+1/k_T$, show the softer element takes the larger share of a given elongation, and recover the velocity split $\dot L_{\text{MTU}}=\dot\ell\cos\theta_p+\dot x$ and the rigid limit. Probes: §4.
Solution
Series elements share force $F$ and add elongations: $x_{\text{tot}}=F/k_M+F/k_T$, so $1/k=1/k_M+1/k_T$. The share of each is $F/k_i$, larger for the smaller $k_i$ — the compliant tendon stretches more. Differentiating the length constraint $L_{\text{MTU}}=\ell\cos\theta_p+L_{Ts}+x$ gives Eq. 4.4, $\dot L_{\text{MTU}}=\dot\ell\cos\theta_p+\dot x$; as $k_T\to\infty$, $\dot x=\dot F/k_T\to0$ and all the length change falls on the fibre (Module 5's rigid tendon).
D6. From the Maxwell ODE (Eq. 6.1) derive the relaxation modulus $G(t)=E_Me^{-t/\tau}$ under a step strain, and show the creep under a step stress is unbounded. Probes: §6.
Solution
Step strain $\varepsilon=\varepsilon_0H(t)$ gives $\dot\varepsilon=0$ for $t\gt0$, so $\dot\sigma+(E_M/\eta)\sigma=0\Rightarrow\sigma=\sigma_0e^{-t/\tau}$ with $\tau=\eta/E_M$ and $\sigma_0=E_M\varepsilon_0$; thus $G(t)=\sigma/\varepsilon_0=E_Me^{-t/\tau}$, decaying to zero (full relaxation). Under step stress $\sigma_0$, $\dot\varepsilon=\dot\sigma/E_M+\sigma/\eta=\sigma_0/\eta$, so $\varepsilon=\varepsilon_{\text{el}}+(\sigma_0/\eta)t$ grows without bound — the dashpot flows forever.
D7. From the Kelvin–Voigt ODE (Eq. 6.2) derive the creep compliance $J(t)=\tfrac{1}{E_K}(1-e^{-t/\tau})$ under a step stress, and show it cannot relax. Probes: §6.
Solution
Step stress $\sigma_0$: $\eta\dot\varepsilon+E_K\varepsilon=\sigma_0$, a first-order linear ODE with solution $\varepsilon(t)=(\sigma_0/E_K)(1-e^{-t/\tau})$, $\tau=\eta/E_K$; so $J=\varepsilon/\sigma_0=\tfrac{1}{E_K}(1-e^{-t/\tau})$, rising to the bounded value $1/E_K$ (bounded creep). Under a step strain, $\dot\varepsilon=0$ so $\sigma=E_K\varepsilon_0$ is constant — no relaxation, because at fixed length the dashpot is idle.
D8. From the SLS ODE (Eq. 6.3) derive the complex modulus $E^\ast(\omega)=E_R\dfrac{1+i\omega\tau_\varepsilon}{1+i\omega\tau_\sigma}$ and the loss tangent, and locate the loss peak. Probes: §7 (Prop. 9).
Solution
Put $\varepsilon=\varepsilon_0e^{i\omega t}$, $\sigma=\sigma_0e^{i\omega t}$ into $\tau_\sigma\dot\sigma+\sigma=E_R(\varepsilon+\tau_\varepsilon\dot\varepsilon)$: $(1+i\omega\tau_\sigma)\sigma_0=E_R(1+i\omega\tau_\varepsilon)\varepsilon_0$, so $E^\ast=\sigma_0/\varepsilon_0=E_R(1+i\omega\tau_\varepsilon)/(1+i\omega\tau_\sigma)$ (Eq. 7.3). Then $\tan\delta=\mathrm{Im}\,E^\ast/\mathrm{Re}\,E^\ast=\omega(\tau_\varepsilon-\tau_\sigma)/(1+\omega^2\tau_\sigma\tau_\varepsilon)$, maximised at $\omega=1/\sqrt{\tau_\sigma\tau_\varepsilon}$ (set $\mathrm{d}\tan\delta/\mathrm{d}\omega=0$).
D9. For a linear viscoelastic material under sinusoidal strain, derive the dissipated energy per cycle $W_d=\oint\sigma\,\mathrm{d}\varepsilon=\pi\sigma_0\varepsilon_0\sin\delta=\pi E''\varepsilon_0^2$. Probes: §7 (Prop. 8).
Solution
With $\varepsilon=\varepsilon_0\sin\omega t$ and $\sigma=\sigma_0\sin(\omega t+\delta)$, $W_d=\int_0^{2\pi/\omega}\sigma\,\dot\varepsilon\,\mathrm{d}t=\sigma_0\varepsilon_0\omega\int_0^{2\pi/\omega}\sin(\omega t+\delta)\cos\omega t\,\mathrm{d}t$. Expanding $\sin(\omega t+\delta)=\sin\omega t\cos\delta+\cos\omega t\sin\delta$, the $\cos^2$ term integrates to $\pi/\omega$ and the cross term to $0$, giving $W_d=\pi\sigma_0\varepsilon_0\sin\delta$. Since $\sigma_0\sin\delta=E''\varepsilon_0$, $W_d=\pi E''\varepsilon_0^2$ (Eq. 7.2): only the out-of-phase part dissipates.
D10. Derive the plantar-fascia tie tension $T=Wb/(4h)$ from the tension-truss model of the arch, and explain how the windlass raises it. Probes: §8 (Prop. 11).
Solution
Model the arch as two rigid struts meeting at the apex, height $h$, base $b$, tied along the base by the fascia (tension $T$). Body load $W$ presses down at the apex; by symmetry each support carries $W/2$. Taking moments about the apex for one half-strut, the vertical reaction $W/2$ at horizontal distance $b/2$ is balanced by $T$ at height $h$: $(W/2)(b/2)=Th$, so $T=Wb/(4h)$ (Eq. 8.2). The windlass — dorsiflexing the toes — wraps the fascia around the metatarsal heads, shortening its free length and pre-tensioning the tie, which raises and stiffens the arch before load even arrives.

Computational (K1–K10)

These require genuine computation — a simulation, an optimisation, an inverse problem, a sensitivity sweep, or a regime comparison — not substitution into a boxed formula. Every boxed number below is printed by the code that follows its solution: copy the block, run it, and check.

K1. Invert a noisy tendon force–elongation dataset: fit the crimp model $F(x)$ (Eq. 2.3) by nonlinear least squares to recover the toe strain $\varepsilon^\ast$ and linear stiffness $k_{\text{lin}}$, and check them against the true values. Probes: §1–§2; inverse problem.
Solution
Fit the two-branch $F(x)$ of Eq. (2.3) to 25 points spanning $1$ to $13\ \mathrm{mm}$ of stretch, generated from $\varepsilon^\ast=3.00\%$ and $k_{\text{lin}}=416\ \mathrm{kN/m}$ (§2) and corrupted with $5\%$ scale noise and a $40\ \mathrm N$ sensor noise floor. Nonlinear least squares returns $\boxed{k_{\text{lin}}=438\pm15\ \mathrm{kN/m},\ \varepsilon^\ast=3.23\pm0.17\%}$, both true values inside one standard error: the two-parameter crimp model is identifiable from a single loading curve, and the fit reports how well. The toe strain is what fixes the curvature of the knee between the parabolic and linear branches; fit a straight line instead and the toe vanishes into an over-stiff low-load region, which is how a stiffness quoted without a toe model can be biased high.
import numpy as np
from scipy.optimize import curve_fit
# inverse problem: recover the crimp model (Eq. 2.3) from noisy F-x data
L0 = 0.25             # tendon rest length (m), Appendix
k_true, e_true = 4.16e5, 0.030   # true k_lin (N/m) and toe strain


def F(x, k_lin, x_star):     # Eq. 2.3, both branches
    return np.where(x <= x_star, k_lin*x**2/(2*x_star),
                    k_lin*(x - x_star/2))


rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
xd = np.linspace(0.001, 0.013, 25)          # 1 to 13 mm of stretch
yd = (F(xd, k_true, e_true*L0)*(1 + 0.05*rng.standard_normal(25))
      + 40*rng.standard_normal(25))          # 5% scale + 40 N sensor noise
p, cov = curve_fit(F, xd, yd, p0=[3.0e5, 0.005], maxfev=20000)
sd = np.sqrt(np.diag(cov))
print(f"k_lin = {p[0]/1e3:.1f} +/- {sd[0]/1e3:.1f} kN/m "
      f"(true {k_true/1e3:.0f})")
print(f"eps*  = {p[1]/L0*100:.2f} +/- {sd[1]/L0*100:.2f} %  "
      f"(true {e_true*100:.2f})")
K2. Compare regimes: a linear tendon and a toe (nonlinear) tendon both reach the same peak force $F_{\text{pk}}=4\ \mathrm{kN}$. By numerical integration of $\int F\,\mathrm{d}x$, which stores more energy, and by how much? Probes: §3; regime comparison + integration.
Solution
To reach $4\ \mathrm{kN}$ the linear spring stretches $9.62\ \mathrm{mm}$ and, integrating $\int F\,\mathrm dx$ numerically, stores $U_{\text{lin}}=19.23\ \mathrm{J}$; the toe tendon must stretch further, $13.37\ \mathrm{mm}$, because its compliant toe shifts the linear branch out by $x^\ast/2$, and stores $\boxed{U_{\text{toe}}=20.21\ \mathrm{J}}$, $\mathbf{5.1\%}$ more for the same peak force. The toe is not only protective: the extra low-force excursion banks additional energy at no additional stress, because stress is force per area and the force is capped by the same $4\ \mathrm{kN}$ in both cases.
import numpy as np
# regime comparison: linear versus toe tendon at one peak force
k_lin, x_star, F_pk = 4.16e5, 0.0075, 4000.0    # N/m, m, N


def F_toe(x):                                   # Eq. 2.3
    return np.where(x <= x_star, k_lin*x**2/(2*x_star),
                    k_lin*(x - x_star/2))


x_lin = F_pk/k_lin                              # linear spring, F = k x
x_toe = F_pk/k_lin + x_star/2                   # invert the linear branch
U = {}
for name, xm, law in (("linear", x_lin, lambda z: k_lin*z),
                      ("toe", x_toe, F_toe)):
    grid = np.linspace(0.0, xm, 200001)
    U[name] = np.trapezoid(law(grid), grid)     # numerical integral of F dx
    print(f"{name:6s}: stretch {xm*1e3:.2f} mm   U = {U[name]:.2f} J")
print(f"the toe tendon stores {100*(U['toe']/U['linear'] - 1):.1f}% more "
      f"at the same peak force")
K3. Model the MTU as a nonlinear muscle passive element in series with the tendon spring. At each imposed stretch, root-find the force balance $F_{PE}(\delta)=k_T(S-\delta)$ for the fibre/tendon split, and sweep $k_T$ to show the fibre's share of the stretch $\to100\%$ (the rigid limit) as $k_T\to\infty$. Probes: §4; implicit solve + known-limit validation (Prop. 4).
Solution
Take the passive fibre law $F_{PE}(\delta)=A\big(e^{\delta/b}-1\big)$ with $A=60\ \mathrm N$ and $b=5\ \mathrm{mm}$, and a total muscle–tendon stretch $S=15\ \mathrm{mm}$ (all assumed; Appendix). The balance $F_{PE}(\delta)=k_T(S-\delta)$ has no closed form, so each stiffness needs a one-dimensional root find. The fibre then carries $\boxed{44.3\%}$ of the stretch for a soft tendon ($k_T=20\ \mathrm{kN/m}$), $70.7\%$ at $100\ \mathrm{kN/m}$, $93.7\%$ at $1000\ \mathrm{kN/m}$ and $99.9\%$ at $10^{5}\ \mathrm{kN/m}$, approaching $100\%$ as $k_T\to\infty$: the series model reduces numerically to Module 5's rigid tendon (Prop. 4). The complement, the tendon's share of the elongation, is exactly the stretch the rigid model refuses to have, and so exactly the elastic energy it throws away.
import numpy as np
from scipy.optimize import brentq
# implicit fibre/tendon split, and the k_T -> infinity limit (Prop. 4)
A, b = 60.0, 0.005      # assumed passive-fibre law F_PE = A(exp(d/b) - 1)
S = 0.015               # assumed total MTU stretch (m)


def fibre_share(k_T):   # root-find F_PE(delta) = k_T (S - delta)
    d = brentq(lambda z: A*(np.exp(z/b) - 1) - k_T*(S - z), 0.0, S)
    return 100*d/S


for k_T in (2.0e4, 1.0e5, 1.0e6, 1.0e8):
    print(f"k_T = {k_T/1e3:9.1f} kN/m -> fibre carries "
          f"{fibre_share(k_T):5.1f}% of the stretch")
K4. A bouncing gait is a driven damped spring–mass. Optimise the leg-spring stiffness for maximum steady energy return at a $2.6\ \mathrm{Hz}$ stride, and show the optimum is the resonant $k^\ast=M\omega^2$ — detuning either way loses return. Probes: §4; optimisation (resonance tuning).
Solution
Write the bounce as a driven damped oscillator, $M\ddot X+c\dot X+kX=F_0\sin\omega t$, with $M=80\ \mathrm{kg}$ (the body mass assumed throughout §9), $\omega=2\pi(2.6)\ \mathrm{rad/s}$, and damping set by a per-cycle resilience $R=0.93$, mid-band of Def. 5, which gives $\zeta=(1-R)/4\pi=0.0056$. The steady amplitude $X(k)=F_0/\sqrt{(k-M\omega^2)^2+(c\omega)^2}$ is largest where the elastic and inertial terms cancel, $\boxed{k^\ast=M\omega^2=21.3\ \mathrm{kN/m}}$. Note that $X$ depends on $k$ only through $|k-M\omega^2|$, so the loss is symmetric in detuning: the sweep prints $0.111$ of peak amplitude at $k=0.90k^\ast$ and again at $1.10k^\ast$, and $0.022$ at $0.50k^\ast$ and $1.50k^\ast$. Amplitude falls to $1/\sqrt2$ of peak at $k=(1\pm2\zeta)k^\ast$, a half-power band $4\zeta=2.2\%$ wide. Read that sharpness as a limit of the model, not of the leg: a real stance also loses energy to muscle work, soft-tissue damping and the step-to-step collision, all of which raise $\zeta$ and widen the band in the same proportion, while leaving $k^\ast$ where it is. That is why leg stiffness tracks gait frequency, and why a mismatch is costly.
import numpy as np
# optimisation: tune the leg spring to the stride frequency
M, f_stride = 80.0, 2.6          # body mass (kg, assumed), stride rate (Hz)
w = 2*np.pi*f_stride
k_star = M*w**2                  # resonant stiffness
zeta = 0.07/(4*np.pi)            # from R = 0.93 per cycle (Def. 5)
c = 2*zeta*np.sqrt(k_star*M)
print(f"k* = M w^2 = {k_star/1e3:.1f} kN/m   zeta = {zeta:.4f}")
print(f"half-power half-width dk/k* = 2 zeta = {2*zeta*100:.1f}% "
      f"(full band 4 zeta = {4*zeta*100:.1f}%)")
for fac in (0.50, 0.75, 0.90, 1 - 2*zeta, 1.00, 1 + 2*zeta, 1.10, 1.50):
    k = fac*k_star
    amp = (c*w)/np.hypot(k - M*w**2, c*w)   # amplitude, as a fraction of peak
    print(f"  k = {fac:.4f} k*  ->  amplitude {amp:.3f} of peak")
K5. Invert a noisy stress-relaxation curve: integrate the SLS law (Eq. 6.3) and least-squares fit to recover $\tau_\sigma,\tau_\varepsilon,E_R$. Probes: §6; inverse problem.
Solution
Fit the SLS step-strain response $\sigma(t)=\varepsilon_0\big[E_R+(E_{\text{inst}}-E_R)e^{-t/\tau_\sigma}\big]$, with $E_{\text{inst}}=E_R\tau_\varepsilon/\tau_\sigma$ from Prop. 7, to 60 samples of a curve generated at $\tau_\sigma=0.050\ \mathrm s$, $\tau_\varepsilon=0.090\ \mathrm s$, $E_R=1.20\ \mathrm{GPa}$ with $2\%$ multiplicative noise. Least squares returns $\boxed{E_R=1.203\ \mathrm{GPa},\ \tau_\sigma=0.0480\ \mathrm s,\ \tau_\varepsilon=0.0866\ \mathrm s}$, hence $E_{\text{inst}}=2.168\ \mathrm{GPa}$ against a true $2.16$. Three features of the curve carry the three constants: the height of the instantaneous jump fixes $E_{\text{inst}}$, the late plateau fixes $E_R$, and the decay rate fixes $\tau_\sigma$. The fourth constant, $\tau_\varepsilon$, is not independent — it is $\tau_\sigma E_{\text{inst}}/E_R$ — which is why a single relaxation test suffices.
import numpy as np
from scipy.optimize import curve_fit
# inverse problem: recover E_R, tau_sigma, tau_eps from a noisy relaxation
e0 = 0.01                                   # imposed strain step
ts_t, te_t, ER_t = 0.050, 0.090, 1.20e9     # true values (s, s, Pa)


def relax(t, ER, ts, te):
    """SLS step-strain response; E_inst = ER te/ts (Prop. 7)."""
    return e0*(ER + ER*(te/ts - 1.0)*np.exp(-t/ts))


rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
td = np.linspace(0.002, 0.5, 60)
sd = relax(td, ER_t, ts_t, te_t)*(1 + 0.02*rng.standard_normal(60))
q, _ = curve_fit(relax, td, sd, p0=[1.0e9, 0.04, 0.07], maxfev=20000)
print(f"E_R = {q[0]/1e9:.3f} GPa (true {ER_t/1e9:.2f})")
print(f"tau_sigma = {q[1]:.4f} s (true {ts_t}), "
      f"tau_eps = {q[2]:.4f} s (true {te_t})")
print(f"E_inst = E_R tau_eps/tau_sigma = {q[0]*q[2]/q[1]/1e9:.3f} GPa "
      f"(true {ER_t*te_t/ts_t/1e9:.2f})")
K6. Integrate Maxwell, Kelvin–Voigt, and SLS under one strain history (ramp to $2\%$, then hold) and compare: which reproduces both an instantaneous response and a partial relaxation? Probes: §6; regime comparison.
Solution
Drive all three models with one history: a $20\ \mathrm{ms}$ ramp to $\varepsilon_0=2\%$, then a $0.6\ \mathrm s$ hold. Use the module's own tendon constants, $E_R=1.20\ \mathrm{GPa}$, $E_{\text{inst}}=2.16\ \mathrm{GPa}$, $\tau_\sigma=0.050\ \mathrm s$ (K5, Appendix), so $\eta=(E_{\text{inst}}-E_R)\tau_\sigma$; give Maxwell the spring $E_M=E_{\text{inst}}$ and Kelvin–Voigt the spring $E_K=E_R$. Integrating each law: Maxwell peaks at $28.5\ \mathrm{MPa}$ and relaxes to $0.0\ \mathrm{MPa}$; Kelvin–Voigt spikes to $72.0\ \mathrm{MPa}$ during the ramp (that spike is pure $\eta\dot\varepsilon$, and it would be unbounded for a true step) and then sits at $E_K\varepsilon_0=24.0\ \mathrm{MPa}$ for ever; the SLS peaks at $39.8\ \mathrm{MPa}$, short of its ideal step value $E_{\text{inst}}\varepsilon_0=43.2\ \mathrm{MPa}$ because it already relaxes during the ramp, then decays to the finite plateau $\boxed{E_R\varepsilon_0=24.0\ \mathrm{MPa}}$. Only the SLS shows both signatures at once, an immediate stiffness and a partial, bounded relaxation (§6).
import numpy as np
# regime comparison: three models under one ramp-and-hold strain history
ER, E_inst, ts = 1.20e9, 2.16e9, 0.050      # SLS constants (K5, Appendix)
eta = (E_inst - ER)*ts                       # dashpot viscosity (Pa s)
EM, EK = E_inst, ER                          # Maxwell and KV spring moduli
e0, t_ramp, t_end, dt = 0.02, 0.02, 0.60, 1.0e-5
sM = sS = sK = 0.0
pk = {"Maxwell": 0.0, "Kelvin-Voigt": 0.0, "SLS": 0.0}
for i in range(int(t_end/dt)):
    t = i*dt
    ed = e0/t_ramp if t < t_ramp else 0.0
    e = min(e0, e0*t/t_ramp)
    sM += dt*(EM*ed - sM*EM/eta)                      # Eq. 6.1
    sK = EK*e + eta*ed                                # Eq. 6.2
    sS += dt*((ER*(e + (ts*E_inst/ER)*ed) - sS)/ts)   # Eq. 6.3
    for nm, v in (("Maxwell", sM), ("Kelvin-Voigt", sK), ("SLS", sS)):
        pk[nm] = max(pk[nm], v)
for nm, fin in (("Maxwell", sM), ("Kelvin-Voigt", sK), ("SLS", sS)):
    print(f"{nm:13s} peak {pk[nm]/1e6:5.1f} MPa -> plateau "
          f"{fin/1e6:5.1f} MPa")
print(f"for reference E_inst e0 = {E_inst*e0/1e6:.1f} MPa, "
      f"E_R e0 = {ER*e0/1e6:.1f} MPa")
K7. Sweep the cycling frequency for an SLS and compute the loop area $W_d$ and loss tangent $\tan\delta$; locate the loss peak $\omega=1/\sqrt{\tau_\sigma\tau_\varepsilon}$. Probes: §7; sensitivity sweep.
Solution
Sweep $\omega$ over six decades through Eq. (7.3) with $\tau_\sigma=0.05\ \mathrm s$, $\tau_\varepsilon=0.10\ \mathrm s$, $E_R=1.20\ \mathrm{GPa}$ and $\varepsilon_0=1\%$. The loop area $W_d=\pi E''\varepsilon_0^2$ and $\tan\delta$ both rise and fall as $\omega$ crosses the material's internal clock, but they peak at different frequencies. The sweep locates the $\tan\delta$ maximum at $\boxed{\omega^\ast=14.13\ \mathrm{rad/s}}$ against the predicted $1/\sqrt{\tau_\sigma\tau_\varepsilon}=14.14$, with $\tan\delta_{\max}=0.354$ and, there, $W_d=177.6\ \mathrm{kJ/m^3}$ per cycle; $W_d$ itself peaks later, at $\omega=1/\tau_\sigma=20\ \mathrm{rad/s}$ where $E''$ is largest, $W_d=\pi E_R(\tau_\varepsilon-\tau_\sigma)\varepsilon_0^2/(2\tau_\sigma)=188.5\ \mathrm{kJ/m^3}$. Two decades either side the tissue is nearly lossless: $\tan\delta=0.005$ at $0.1\ \mathrm{rad/s}$ and $0.010$ at $1000\ \mathrm{rad/s}$. Dissipation is a resonance of the internal clock, not a monotone property of speed. Now note where that peak lands: $f^\ast=2.25\ \mathrm{Hz}$ is running cadence. This is the fast mode, the one the labs use because it settles inside a short simulation; the modes that dominate a real tendon are slower by one to three decades, which is what puts gait on the low-loss side (§7, Appendix).
import numpy as np
# sensitivity sweep: where does an SLS lose the most energy per cycle?
ts, te, e0 = 0.050, 0.100, 0.01   # tau_sigma, tau_eps (s), strain amplitude
ER = 1.20e9


def moduli(w):                    # Eq. 7.3
    Es = ER*(1 + 1j*w*te)/(1 + 1j*w*ts)
    return Es.real, Es.imag


w = np.logspace(-2, 4, 4001)
Ep, Epp = moduli(w)
tand = Epp/Ep
Wd = np.pi*Epp*e0**2              # Eq. 7.2, per unit volume
i = int(tand.argmax())
print(f"loss peak at w = {w[i]:.2f} rad/s (predicted "
      f"{1/np.sqrt(ts*te):.2f}), f = {w[i]/(2*np.pi):.2f} Hz")
print(f"tan delta_max = {tand[i]:.3f}, W_d there = "
      f"{Wd[i]/1e3:.1f} kJ/m^3 per cycle")
for wq in (0.10, 14.14, 1000.0):
    a, bq = moduli(wq)
    print(f"  w = {wq:8.2f} rad/s: tan delta = {bq/a:.4f}")
K8. By loop integration, compute the energy-return resilience of a low-loss (tendon) and a high-loss (ligament) tissue across the running-cadence band, and compare. Probes: §7; regime comparison + sweep.
Solution
Impose a tension-only cycle $\varepsilon(t)=\tfrac12\varepsilon_0(1-\cos\omega t)$ at a cadence of $2.6\ \mathrm{Hz}$, integrate Eq. (6.3) to steady state, and take the resilience as work recovered on the unloading half divided by work done on the loading half. Holding $\tau_\sigma=0.05\ \mathrm s$ fixed, the spread between the two time constants alone sorts the tissues: $\tau_\varepsilon/\tau_\sigma=1.10$ returns $\boxed{92.6\%}$ (hysteresis $7.4\%$) and $\tau_\varepsilon/\tau_\sigma=1.20$ returns $85.7\%$ (hysteresis $14.3\%$). Those are the tendon row and the ligament row of the table in §7, reproduced from the constitutive law rather than quoted. The governing equation never changes; widening the gap between $\tau_\varepsilon$ and $\tau_\sigma$ alone turns an energy-return spring into a damper, which is the quantitative face of C9.
import numpy as np
# regime comparison: energy return of a low-loss and a high-loss tissue
ER, e0, f = 1.20e9, 0.01, 2.6     # Pa, strain amplitude, cadence (Hz)
ts = 0.050                        # tau_sigma (s)


def resilience(te, ncyc=8, dt=1.0e-5):
    """Integrate Eq. 6.3 over a tension-only cycle; return W_out/W_in."""
    w, per, s = 2*np.pi*f, 1.0/f, 0.0
    w_in = w_out = 0.0
    n = int(per/dt)
    for cyc in range(ncyc):
        for i in range(n):
            t = i*dt
            e = 0.5*e0*(1 - np.cos(w*t))
            ed = 0.5*e0*w*np.sin(w*t)
            s += dt*((ER*(e + te*ed) - s)/ts)
            if cyc == ncyc - 1:
                if ed > 0:
                    w_in += s*ed*dt
                else:
                    w_out -= s*ed*dt
    return w_out/w_in


for name, ratio in (("tendon", 1.10), ("ligament", 1.20)):
    R = resilience(ts*ratio)
    print(f"{name:9s} tau_eps/tau_sigma = {ratio}: R = {100*R:.1f}%, "
          f"hysteresis {100*(1 - R):.1f}%")
K9. Simulate the knee crossed-cruciate four-bar over the flexion arc: solve for the tibial link position (both cruciate lengths fixed), find the instant centre as the cruciate crossing, and trace the centrode. Quantify its migration. Probes: §8; kinematic simulation.
Solution
Fix the geometry: femoral attachments at $A_f=(0,0)$ and $P_f=(-20,0)\ \mathrm{mm}$, an ACL of $32\ \mathrm{mm}$, a PCL of $34\ \mathrm{mm}$, and a rigid tibial link of $28\ \mathrm{mm}$ joining their tibial ends (assumed; Appendix). With these values the ACL meets the tibial link, which lies along the tibial plateau, at $45^\circ$ at full extension, the order of the anatomical sagittal inclination of the ACL to the tibial plateau (about $45^\circ$), so the knee figures draw the ligament at a realistic slope. For each tibial orientation one root find places the linkage with both cruciate lengths held fixed, and the instant centre is the intersection of the two cruciate lines (Prop. 10). The crossing stays inside both ligaments throughout, moving from $42\%$ along the ACL at full extension to $15\%$ at $60^\circ$, so it is a real crossing and not an extension of the lines outside the joint. The centre itself travels from $(-9.4,-9.4)\ \mathrm{mm}$ to $(-0.1,-4.6)\ \mathrm{mm}$: an arc length of $10.9\ \mathrm{mm}$ and a net migration of $\boxed{10.5\ \mathrm{mm}}$ over $60^\circ$ of flexion, posteriorly and proximally. A fixed-hinge knee would hold one point. The migrating centre is why the femur rolls back on the tibia as it flexes (§8).
import numpy as np
from scipy.optimize import brentq
# kinematic simulation: the crossed-cruciate four-bar and its centrode
Af, Pf = np.array([0.0, 0.0]), np.array([-20.0, 0.0])   # femoral link (mm)
L_ACL, L_PCL, L_tib = 32.0, 34.0, 28.0                  # assumed lengths (mm)


def pose(th):
    """Place the tibial link at orientation th; both cruciates rigid."""
    def gap(s):
        At = Af + L_ACL*np.array([np.cos(s), np.sin(s)])
        Pt = At + L_tib*np.array([np.cos(th), np.sin(th)])
        return float(np.hypot(*(Pt - Pf)) - L_PCL)
    s = brentq(gap, np.radians(-160), np.radians(-20))
    At = Af + L_ACL*np.array([np.cos(s), np.sin(s)])
    return At, At + L_tib*np.array([np.cos(th), np.sin(th)])


def cross(p1, p2, p3, p4):
    """Intersect lines p1p2 and p3p4; also return both line parameters."""
    r, s = p2 - p1, p4 - p3
    d = r[0]*s[1] - r[1]*s[0]
    u = ((p3[0] - p1[0])*s[1] - (p3[1] - p1[1])*s[0])/d
    v = ((p3[0] - p1[0])*r[1] - (p3[1] - p1[1])*r[0])/d
    return p1 + u*r, u, v


C = []
for j, th in enumerate(np.radians(np.linspace(0.0, 60.0, 61))):
    At, Pt = pose(th)
    I, u, v = cross(Af, At, Pf, Pt)
    C.append(I)
    if j in (0, 60):
        print(f"{np.degrees(th):4.0f} deg: crossing at ACL fraction "
              f"{u:.2f}, PCL fraction {v:.2f}")
C = np.array(C)
arc = float(np.hypot(*np.diff(C, axis=0).T).sum())
print(f"instant centre ({C[0][0]:.1f}, {C[0][1]:.1f}) mm at 0 deg -> "
      f"({C[-1][0]:.1f}, {C[-1][1]:.1f}) mm at 60 deg")
print(f"centrode arc length {arc:.1f} mm, net migration "
      f"{np.hypot(*(C[-1] - C[0])):.1f} mm")
K10. Over a stance phase with a half-sine vertical load (peak $2.5\times$ body weight), integrate the plantar-fascia arch's stored elastic energy and compare its contribution to the Achilles. Probes: §8; integration + regime comparison.
Solution
Impose a half-sine vertical load peaking at $2.5$ body weights on an $80\ \mathrm{kg}$ body (the mass assumed throughout §9), pass it through the truss relation $T=Wb/(4h)$ with $b=0.15\ \mathrm m$ and $h=0.05\ \mathrm m$, and load a linear tie of stiffness $k_{PF}=2\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{N/m}$ (Appendix). The peak tie tension is $1.47\ \mathrm{kN}$, the fascia stretches $7.36\ \mathrm{mm}$, and the tie banks $\boxed{5.41\ \mathrm J}$ at peak load, against the Achilles' $32\ \mathrm J$ (§3): $14\%$ of the pair. Read the gap to §0 carefully. The $\sim17\ \mathrm J$ quoted there is an unverified literature figure for the whole arch, every plantar ligament and the joint capsules together; this model has one tie, so a smaller number is the expected result, not a discrepancy. The single-tie truss is a lower bound on the arch's elastic return. Even at that bound, ignoring the arch under-counts the free elastic return of the leg by about a seventh (§8).
import numpy as np
# integration: elastic energy banked by the plantar-fascia tie over stance
M, g = 80.0, 9.81            # body mass (kg, assumed), gravity
b, h = 0.15, 0.05            # arch base and height (m), Appendix
k_PF = 2.0e5                 # plantar-fascia stiffness (N/m), Appendix
t = np.linspace(0.0, 1.0, 20001)
W = 2.5*M*g*np.sin(np.pi*t)  # half-sine vertical load, peak 2.5 body weights
T = W*b/(4*h)                # Eq. 8.2
x = T/k_PF
U = 0.5*T*x                  # equals the integral of k_PF x dx for a tie
print(f"peak load {W.max():.0f} N = {W.max()/(M*g):.1f} body weights")
print(f"peak tie tension {T.max()/1e3:.2f} kN, stretch {x.max()*1e3:.2f} mm")
print(f"peak stored energy {U.max():.2f} J; with the Achilles at 32 J (S3) "
      f"the tie is {100*U.max()/(U.max() + 32):.0f}% of the pair")

That closes Module 6. From the crimp of a single collagen fibril we have built, step by verifiable step, the tendon as a nonlinear spring, the energy it banks and returns, its series coupling to the muscle and the catapult that follows, the viscoelastic creep and hysteresis that make it imperfect, and the ligaments, fascia and arch that constrain and store. The passive tissues are no longer the rigid constraints Module 3 assumed nor the inextensible tendon Module 5 assumed — they are springs, and the debts are paid. What remains — the whole-body bounce, the slow accrual of damage, the three-dimensional continuum — is written into Modules 9, 14 and 16 (Fig. 24).

Appendix — notation and parameters

Every symbol introduced in the module, grouped by role and linked to the section that defines it, followed by representative healthy-adult parameter values. This module builds on Module 1 (energy and levers), Module 3 (joints as constraints), and Module 5 (the Hill-type muscle it pulls against), and hands its idealisations forward to Modules 9, 14 and 16 (§10, Fig. 24).

Values are round representative figures for orientation, not patient-specific data; each varies with tissue, individual, training, hydration, and measurement method (§10). The wide range of viscoelastic time constants is why a single tendon can look like a near-perfect spring at running frequencies yet creep visibly over minutes (§6).
